storyboard.claim: Humbert's art is a literary prison — the road trip ended but the artistic cage keeps Dolores trapped forever.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon — she is imprisoned, locked in his writing. Humbert sits writing at a desk while Dolores stands behind, bound by the art he creates.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From 'my Lolita' (ownership) to the mechanism of that ownership: the manuscript itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains make the 'cage' concrete — without sound, a viewer reads imprisonment. Humbert holds the notes (the confession) that keep her locked.

storyboard.claim: The confession is one last act of seduction — Humbert is controlling the reader through his pretty book.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Puppeteer icon — one person controlling others. Humbert addresses the reader-jury from the courtroom, pulling strings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the cage (what the art does to Dolores) to what the art does to the reader.
storyboard.addedInformation: The puppeteer makes visible who is being manipulated: us.

storyboard.claim: If you feel sorry for Humbert and think his love was profound, the trap has worked on you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: No icon — the struck-through phrase carries the rejection. Humbert slumps looking pitiable; the strike tells the viewer this sympathy is the wrong reading.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Humbert as puppeteer to the specific thought he plants: pity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike rejects the sympathetic reading. His sad posture is the seduction itself — he LOOKS pitiable on purpose.

storyboard.claim: The trap: seductive rhetoric can manufacture consent for the inexcusable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Funnel-trap icon — the narrator literally says 'That's the trap.' The icon shows the reader being funneled into consenting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the struck-out sympathetic reading to the thesis it proves: consent can be manufactured.
storyboard.addedInformation: The trap icon literalises the narrator's own word. The thesis statement lands visually.

storyboard.claim: Synthesis: Humbert's con followed a chain — spell, fake backstory, road-trip kidnapping, silencing, confession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram showing the five stages of Humbert's seduction strategy, the hosts' own recap structure.
storyboard.onScreenText: None — the diagram labels carry the recap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The thesis has landed; now the hosts walk back through the whole journey.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram compresses the entire arc into one visible chain so the muted viewer sees the shape of the argument.

storyboard.claim: Humbert used Dante, Petrarch, and Poe as a literary shield to build a fake origin story.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon in the courtroom — the origin story is a fabrication, a false face. Humbert stands alone, worried, caught.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First item in the recap: the Annabel backstory and its literary shielding.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask + courtroom + worried expression reads as exposure/fabrication, not romance.

storyboard.claim: Humbert used the geography of America to disguise a kidnapping as a road trip.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon on the highway — the road trip is imprisonment. Dolores slumps alone, sad, trapped.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second recap item: the road-trip kidnapping, after the fake origin.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains + sad slumping Dolores alone on highway reads as captivity, not a romantic journey.

storyboard.claim: He silenced the real Dolores — the girl who cried in her sleep — and buried her under the myth of a nymph.
storyboard.concreteVisual: No icon — the image is Dolores herself, the silenced victim. She slumps alone in the bedroom, crying.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Third recap item: from the road that trapped her to the girl it silenced.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dolores alone with no icon is the point — her real self is the thing Humbert erased. The bedroom makes 'in her sleep' literal.

storyboard.claim: The confession is fake — performing remorse to lock Dolores in a literary cage forever.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mask icon — Humbert's performed remorse is a false face. He sits writing in his cell, looking sad, but the mask tells the viewer the sadness is worn, not felt.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Final recap item: from the silenced Dolores to the confession that pretends to mourn her.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask over his sad expression says: this grief is a performance. He holds the notes — the weapon.

storyboard.claim: Lolita is not just controversial — it is a masterclass in critical thinking and media literacy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Book icon — the beat is literally about the novel itself. Nabokov holds the book he built.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Humbert's fake confession to why the whole novel matters: Nabokov built a teaching tool.
storyboard.addedInformation: Nabokov appears for the first time in the chunk — the architect behind the trap, shifting credit from character to author.

storyboard.claim: The novel trains you to look past beautiful delivery and interrogate the horrific truths rhetoric can hide.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Magnifier icon — close examination. Nabokov holds a magnifier, training the reader to scrutinise.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the book as masterclass to the specific skill it teaches: close examination.
storyboard.addedInformation: The magnifier makes 'interrogate' visual — the lesson is about seeing through surfaces.

storyboard.claim: You, the intelligent reader, can become complicit in a narrative if it is packaged attractively enough.
storyboard.concreteVisual: No icon — the accusation is aimed at the viewer. Nabokov points outward with a worried expression: you are not safe from this.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the skill the novel teaches to the warning: even you can be fooled.
storyboard.addedInformation: Nabokov's worried face and pointing gesture say this is a warning, not a lecture. No icon because the subject is the viewer, not an object.

storyboard.claim: How many beautiful stories in news, history, media are actually crime scenes hiding in plain sight?
storyboard.concreteVisual: No icon — the beat is about narratives beyond the book, and no single icon covers 'all media.' Nabokov points outward, extending the lesson.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From your complicity in this novel to every narrative you consume.
storyboard.addedInformation: The callout carries the beat — 'crime scenes in plain sight' is the narrator's own reframing of all media. weak: two consecutive Nabokov-pointing beats, but the subject broadens from 'you' to 'everything you read.'

storyboard.claim: Look past the silk sentences and see the victim underneath.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores alone, standing still — the real person the entire novel buried. No icon because she IS the answer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From 'crime scenes in plain sight' to the specific victim of this one: Dolores.
storyboard.addedInformation: The final image is the girl herself — quiet, sad, present. After 213 beats of Humbert's rhetoric, she is the last thing you see.
